newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: ANOTHER POLITICIAN'S EXPENSE ACCOUNT INVESTIGATED
National Party MP, Michael Cobb, says he's confident he'll be fully cleared by an investigation into his use of parliamentary expenses.
Mr Cobb returned to Sydney from Papua New Guinea last night saying politicians tend to be targets of cheap allegations and vexatious claims.
He says he met with the Australian Federal Police last September and assisted them in their investigations.
Liberal Senator Bob Woods is also having his use of parliamentary expenses investigated.
Opposition leader Kim Beazley says when it comes to standards of accountabilty this has been the messiest first 10 months for a Government in his memory.
The Prime Minister says he was briefed on the allegations against Mr Cobb last August but both he and Senator Woods are entitled to the presumption of innocence.
INDUSTRY CALLS FOR TAX CUTS TO BE ABANDONED
A leading business group wants the Federal Government to scrap the promised four-billion dollars in tax cuts.
The Chamber of Commerce and Industry says this will enable the three-billion dollar budget deficit to be reduced without cutting more business assistance programmes.
The Government has so far said it will honor the tax cuts which were promised by the former Labor Government as a superannuation contribution.
But the Coalition hasn't revealed how and when the cuts will be delivered.
FOOD DROP IN SOUTH AUSTRALIA
A helicopter is this morning going to rescue nine tourists stranded by floodwaters west of Anna Creek in South Australia's far north.
The tourists spent the night in a maksehift roadaside camp.
Sixteen residents stranded at the Anna Creek homestead have so far refused assistance, but police say the group may have to be rescued today.
Food parcels will be dropped this morning in the region's worst affected areas.
ABORIGINES OFFERED INCENTIVES TO BACK GAS PIPELINE
Aboriginal elders on the New South Wales south coast have been offered financial support for small business and educational scholarships if they support the Eastern Gas Pipeline project.
Project consortium BHP and West Coast Energy want to bring natural gas from Bass Strait to Sydney and regional centres such as Nowra and Wollongong.
The consortium has offered to establish small business trust funds of 80-thousand-dollars a year, as well as scholarships worth up to 20-thousand-dollars a year per student.
Reuben Brown of the South Coast Tribal Elders Corporation says the package was given in-principal endorsement over the weekend and should get formal consent this week.
DEMOCRATS SAY WORK FOR DOLE SCHEME A STOP GAP MEASURE
The Australian Democrats say young people should be given education and training opportunities instead of being made to work for the dole.
Prime Minister, John Howard, says the Government is considering running pilot work-for-the-dole schemes in rural and regional areas with high unemployment.
But Democrats Employment and Training spokeswoman, Natasha Stott-Despoja, says that's a short-term stop-gap measure.
Senator Stott-Despoya says the experience people gain through abour market programmes leads to longer term jobs in the future.
She also says structural and technologocal change has to be taken into account in deciding how to help the unemployed.
MORE ANTHRAX CASES IN VICTORIA
There have now been ten cases of anthrax involving 30 cows in the Goulburn Valley in central northern Victoria.
The latest five anthrax outbreaks are on properties between Stanhope and Tatura.
The Natural Resources and Environment Department is investigating the outbreaks, but is yet to find any common link.
The Chief Veterinary Officer, Dr Andrew Turner, says there is no threat to milk products.
GOVT AND ABORIGINES TO HOLD PRELIMINARY WIK TALKS
Federal Government and Aboriginal lawyers will meet early this week on the High Court's Wik native title ruling ahead of the Prime Minister's discussions with all stakeholders on Friday.
Mr Howard's office says the lawyers' meeting is aimed at clearing up a divergence of opinion on the implications of the court ruling, which found native title can co-exist with pastoral leases.
The Prime Minister will meet with stakeholders at the end of the week.
Those discussions are likely to involve two representatives each from the pastoral and mining industries and four Aboriginal leaders.
Mr Howard has said he hopes the meeting will find common ground on a resolution to uncertainty over pastoral leases.
